docs.title: RedGem 3D Engine
docs.text:
RedGem is a 3D game engine with its own editor. You build levels in the editor (or in Blender), write the gameplay in Ruby, press Play, and export a standalone game.

This manual is for people making games with it.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
1. Install the editor.
  2. Follow Your first game: about fifteen minutes from an empty folder to a playable game.
  3. Keep Behaviours and the API reference open while you write scripts.

docs.title: How a game is organized
docs.text:
A game is a folder:

Path What it is scene.glb The main level: objects, meshes, lights, cameras scenes/*.glb More levels scripts/*.rb Ruby behaviours and scene scripts models/*.glb Models you can drop into a level sounds/ .wav, .ogg, .mp3 or .flac files images/ Pictures for menus and the HUD (.png, .jpg) locales/ The texts players read, one translation file per language: en.json, pt.json... (see Texts in several languages) game.json The game's id, title and window size

The editor reads and writes these files directly. There is no project database and no import step: what you see in the folder is the game.

docs.title: Working on the engine
docs.text: For people changing RedGem itself. To make games with it, the rest of this manual is enough.

docs.title: Demos
docs.text:
Demos: games/city (a crossroad with Ruby-driven traffic: lights, braking, spinning wheels; Kenney CC0 models), games/platformer (WASD/arrows, Space jumps: grab 5 coins, reach the flag) and games/driving (W/S throttle, A/D steer, Space hand brake, R reset: drive laps).

Showcase (games/showcase, not committed: it is built from downloaded assets). A street at dusk with a drivable car, traffic that keeps its distance and overtakes, parked cars, shop fronts and cafe tables, a crowd on the sidewalks, potholes and falling leaves, made to push the renderer. Blender only builds the scene; everything that happens in it is set up in games/showcase/scripts/main_scene.rb:

python3 -I tools/assets/fetch_showcase.py      # street: Poly Haven and ambientCG (CC0)
python3 -I tools/assets/fetch_ad_assets.py     # car and people: BlenderKit (see showcase/CREDITS.md)
SHOWCASE_RENDER=0 BLENDER_MEMORY_MAX=8500M tools/blender/run.sh build_showcase.py showcase
./build/src/redgem games/showcase           # then Play: WASD drives, Space brakes

The export needs about 7 GB of memory (close the editor first); without SHOWCASE_RENDER=0 it also renders showcase/renders/ad.png with Cycles, which needs an NVIDIA RTX card. games/city is rebuilt with tools/assets/fetch_kenney.sh and tools/blender/run.sh build_city.py games/city.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
cd build && ctest --output-on-failure        # everything
ctest -L system                              # only the system tests

Tests are run by a program of their own, redgem-test, built beside redgem (see Libraries and programs). A system test is a Ruby file run against a game: redgem-test <game_dir> <file.rb> [--screenshots <dir>] [--headless] [--work <dir>] (--headless runs without a window, --work gives the run a folder of its own for its save file and notes; redgem-test --help lists every option).

The engine knows nothing of tests. Neither redgem nor redgem-player, which is what every built game ships as, has test code in it: what tests are written with (TestInput, SystemTest, RedGemTest, the runners and their command line) lives in src/testing and ruby/testing, a library that only redgem-test links. The engine gives it nothing but general options (EngineOptions: a fixed step per frame, an input fed by code, a save file, who shows the game) and the window a game is shown in tells whoever asks when a frame is drawn; the pictures a test takes (t.screenshot) are written by the test tool from there. Keep it that way: the app.ships_no_test_code test looks into the built redgem-player and redgem and fails when test code got in.

  • C++ unit + integration (doctest): math, extras parser, glTF loading from Blender fixtures, scene hierarchy, physics world, Ruby VM, and an engine nobody shows running the sandbox fixture game (and one shown by a presenter that records what it is handed).
  • Tests of the test tool (tests/testing/, doctest): its command line, its save file, what it adds to a game's Ruby, and whole runs of passing and failing tests.
  • Ruby tests run inside the engine's mruby: redgem-test --ruby tests/ruby/vector3_test.rb.
  • Editor system test (tests/editor_system/) opens the editor window on a copy of the platformer, picks, edits, plays, stops, undoes and saves.
  • System tests (tests/system/<game>/*_test.rb, run against games/<game>) open the real game window and drive it frame by frame with simulated input:
SystemTest.define do |t|
  t.hold(:w, frames: 60)
  t.wait_until(frames: 30) { Scene.find("Coin1").nil? }
  t.assert("score counts the coin") { GameManager.instance.coins == 1 }
  t.screenshot("collect_coin_after")        # saved to build/screenshots/<game>/
end

A template is tested as the game it makes: tests/system_templates/<template>/*_test.rb run against a game created from it by redgem new. Every template needs at least one.

Test fixtures are regenerated with tools/blender/run.sh build_test_fixtures.py tests/fixtures.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
src/core      what everything shares: math, logging, the fixed timestep clock, files, the platform
              layer (the only place, with the sockets of src/net, that asks which system this is),
              the words of a command line, embedding files in the binary, the game folder's layout
              (config.hpp)
src/scene     scene graph (objects, transforms, copies), particles, the custom properties scenes
              carry (props.hpp); in folders of their own: gltf/ (the loader: meshes, skeletons,
              animations, Blender extras), animation/ (clips and their playback), shapes/
              (primitives and terrain)
src/physics   PhysicsWorld interface + Jolt implementation
src/input     keys, axes/actions, keyboard, mouse, gamepad and scripted input sources; a touch
              screen's on-screen controls (touch_input_source.hpp), which only the program for
              a touch screen puts in front of the others
src/net       message framing and wire format, the host/guest session and its connection approval;
              socket/ (the only place with OS socket calls, what the systems spell differently being
              in socket_native), discovery/ (games on the local network), rooms/ (the relay and the
              entry point of its program, relay_main.cpp, and what a dedicated server's rooms share
              with it: codes, the lobby, guessers kept out), http/ (the games' web requests:
              HTTP/1.1 over Mbed TLS, one thread per request)
src/audio     sound effects and music (raylib, or silence when there is no audio device)
src/storage   what a game keeps between runs (the save store)
src/render    the window (window.hpp: the only place that opens one, with its graphics card, frame
              pace and pointer), the renderer that draws in it and owns what is on the card (HDR,
              shadows, reflections, post-processing), shaders, environment, culling, mesh
              conversion, what differs per graphics API (gpu_profile.hpp), the font texts are
              drawn with
src/script    mruby VM, behaviour host, native bindings
src/app       what plays a game: the engine loop, which draws nothing and hands each frame
              (FrameView) to a presenter (presenter.hpp); the presenter that shows a game in a
              window of its own and the painter every drawing presenter shares; game.json, the
              game beside a built executable, where saves go, user settings, the entry points of
              the player (player_main.cpp; on Android, android/android_main.cpp)
src/editor    editor: session (play mode), camera, picking, the app and its panels; document/ (the
              scene document: undo, save, the glb it edits, importing models), scripts/ (the script
              tabs), ui/ (ImGui panels and theme)
src/project   the tools around a game: new games from templates, builds (desktop, and Android in
              android/), recent games and the project hub, the command line, the entry point of
              redgem (main.cpp)
src/testing   what runs tests, apart from the engine: TestInput, the pictures a test takes of the
              game (TestScreen), the system test and Ruby test runners, the audio tests listen
              with, redgem-test and its command line
ruby/engine   Ruby prelude embedded in the runtime (Behaviour, Vector3, UI, Network...)
ruby/testing  the Ruby tests are written with (assertions, test cases, the system test DSL),
              embedded in redgem-test only
templates     the new-game templates: each folder is a whole game (scene, scripts, sounds) and a
              template.json about it, embedded in redgem as it is; a new game is a copy of one.
              A template is edited like any game: redgem templates/platformer
locales      the texts users read, one translation file per language (see Texts users read)
assets/editor fonts of the editor (Inter, JetBrains Mono; SIL Open Font License, see the license files)
games         demo games: scene.glb, scripts and the .blend each scene was built from
showcase      renders of the showcase scene and the credits of its assets
tools/blender scene builders (run with tools/blender/run.sh), walk_rig.py
tools/assets  downloaders of the free assets the demos use
tests         unit, integration, Ruby and system tests, with their fixtures
cmake         dependencies (pinned versions) and file embedding

The folders of src are layers, in the order above: each includes only itself and what is below it (core; then scene, net, input, audio, physics, storage; then render and script; then app; then server, editor, project; testing sees everything and nothing sees it). Each layer keeps its own numbers in a <layer>_config.hpp next to its code.

docs.title: Objects, and keeping hold of one
docs.text:
A scene object's ObjectId is a slot. The loaded scene's objects keep their slots (an id below the node count is that node); the slot of an object made while the game runs (Scene::clone, Scene.spawn) holds a new object once it is destroyed. Every object also gets an ObjectSerial no other object ever had, in any scene.

  • What keeps an object past the step it was handed it (a skin's bones, a vehicle's wheels, a character's own clip, a behaviour, a Ruby GameObject or Transform) keeps an ObjectHandle and asks Scene::resolve for it each time: that finds the object while it is alive, and nothing afterwards, whoever sits in its slot.
  • Only a registry the engine updates in the very step an object is destroyed may key by bare id: the physics bodies (Engine::process_destroyed removes them) and the scene's own hierarchy and copies.
  • Destruction is two steps: request_destroy marks an object and what is under it, its on_destroy runs with everything still there, then the batch is torn down children first.

docs.title: Libraries and programs
docs.text:
The folders are built into a few static libraries, one on top of the other, and each program links only the ones it is made of (src/CMakeLists.txt):

redgem_core     src/core                                           links nothing of the engine's
redgem_net      src/net                                            redgem_core, the JSON library,
                                                                   Mbed TLS
redgem_runtime  scene, physics, audio, input, storage, render,     redgem_net, raylib, Jolt, mruby,
                script, app, and the Ruby prelude                  cgltf, the JSON library
redgem_game_server src/server (without server_main.cpp)            redgem_runtime
redgem_editor   src/editor                                         redgem_runtime, Dear ImGui
redgem_project  src/project (without main.cpp), the templates      redgem_editor
                and the licenses
redgem_testing  src/testing, ruby/testing                          redgem_runtime

redgem-player   src/app/player_main.cpp    redgem_runtime   what players receive: plays the game in
                                                            the game/ folder beside it, nothing else
redgem          src/project/main.cpp       redgem_project   the editor, the project hub, the command
                                                            line (new, build, --play)
redgem-relay    src/net/rooms/relay_main.cpp     redgem_net       the meeting point for games over the
                                                            internet: no window, for servers
redgem-server   src/server/server_main.cpp redgem_game_server
                                                            a game run on a server for players to
                                                            join, in rooms: no window, no display
redgem-test     src/testing/main.cpp       redgem_testing   runs a game's tests
libredgem.so    src/app/android/android_main.cpp   redgem_runtime   the player on Android, loaded by the app

A built game is a copy of the player, never of the program that builds it: redgem build and the editor's Build take redgem-player from beside redgem, or runtimes/<system>/ there for another system (tools/windows/build_runtime.sh, tools/android/build_runtime.sh build those). cmake --install build --component redgem --prefix <folder> puts the five programs in <folder>/bin and the players for other systems in <folder>/bin/runtimes, where the same lookups find them.

Keep what players receive small: nothing the player links may include editor/ or project/ (the include directions below say so, and linking proves it). The tests app.player_ships_no_tools, app.relay_ships_no_game and app.server_ships_no_tools look into the built programs (tests/ships_no_tools.sh) for texts only the tools, or only a game, have.

A program opens one window, through Window, and makes what draws in it afterwards (a Renderer, the editor's ui::Interface): the project hub, the editor and a played game each do. The engine never does: it is given a Presenter. WindowPresenter shows a game in its own window (redgem-player, redgem --play, redgem-test), the editor's Scene view is another (EditorApp::GameView), and without one nobody shows the game (NullPresenter: tests, servers). What a game can show is a field of FrameView, drawn in FramePainter: added there, it reaches every presenter. tests/include_directions.sh holds the table and fails the test suite on an include that goes up.

docs.title: Texts users read
docs.text:
What a user of RedGem reads is not written in the code: it is in translation files, one per language, under locales/<part>/<language>.json, and the code names it by a key (tr("editor.menu.file"), see src/core/translations.hpp). Today there is English (en.json) alone; a translation is another file beside it, with the same keys.

  • Into a translation file: everything a user reads in a window or at a terminal. The editor and the project hub (menus, buttons, panels, tooltips, dialogs, hints, the status bar, the inspector's labels), the help, usage and errors of the command lines of redgem, redgem-server, redgem-relay and redgem-test that are about what the user typed, and the texts the engine shows players (the labels of GameMenu).
  • In English in the code: the log, and the messages of errors that are for whoever works on the engine or a game (a broken file, a failed call). Those are searched for, quoted in bug reports and read next to the code; they stay in one language, as the code does.

Each part is the texts of one library, built into it (redgem_embed_texts in src/CMakeLists.txt), so that a program carries only what it shows: core (what a command line says of an option it cannot read), game (the runtime: what players read), editor, project (the hub and redgem's command line), server, relay and testing (the command lines of the other programs). A program adds its parts and picks the language as it starts: the one in the user's settings ("language" in settings.json), else the system's; a key a translation lacks is shown in English.

A key is the part's name, then where the text is, then what it is: editor.menu.file. The first word says which file it is in. A text with values in it names them, Created {game}, and the code fills them in: tr("project.cli.created", {{"game", name}}). A long text (a command's usage) may be a list of lines. tests/unit/translation_keys_test.cpp fails when the code shows a key English has no text for, when an English text is shown nowhere, or when a translation has a key English lacks; keys are written whole in the code, as string literals, for it to find them.

A game's texts are not the engine's: they are in the game's own locales/<language>.json, and its scripts show them with I18n.t("hud.coins") (see Texts in several languages), behind which are the engine's game part (the prelude's I18n.t calls, in ruby/engine/), so a game's files may translate those too. The same test checks the games and templates of this repository: every key their scripts show has a text in their locales/en.json or the game part, and every text of theirs is shown.

docs.text:

  • Spot light cones, and camera clip planes from the scene (the engine uses fixed ones).
  • Reusing data when the same model is imported twice, and dropping the data of deleted imports from scene.glb (each import appends its meshes and textures).
  • Mirrored objects (negative scale) are drawn inside out.
  • More vehicle options from Blender properties (drive layout, engine torque); hot reload of scripts while playing.

docs.title: Dedicated server
docs.text:
With a dedicated server nobody has to host: the game runs on a machine on the internet, with no window and no player, and everyone joins it, phones included. A small rented Linux server (a VPS) is enough. It needs no display and no graphics card.

The server is a program of its own, redgem-server. One server holds several rooms. Each room is a match of its own, with the whole game running in it. Players join by the server's address and get the first room with a free place, or a new room when every room is full. A friend can follow them into the same room with its code (Network.room). A room closes when its match ends: the game calls Game.quit, or everyone left. The next players get a new room, with a new game.

Nobody runs a server for you: each game runs its own, on a machine its players can reach, as below. The same goes for a relay.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
./build/src/redgem-server games/platformer      # listens on port 7777
./build/src/redgem-server games/platformer --port 9000 --max-players 4 --rooms 16 --data /srv/platformer
Option Default What it is --port 7777 The TCP port players connect to (0 picks a free one) --max-players 8 Players in one room, up to 15 --rooms 8 Rooms open at once, up to 64 --threads The machine's cores Threads the rooms run on, up to 64: each room has one of its own while there are no more rooms than threads --per-address 24 Machines one address may connect, up to 1024: raise it when many players share one address (a campus, some mobile networks) --data <game>-data beside the game's folder Where the game's Save is kept (save.sqlite3), for every room and every run

It writes what happens to its output (rooms opened and closed, how many players) and stops cleanly on Ctrl+C or SIGTERM: every room is closed and its players are told.

A room is light (a platformer room takes 1 to 2 MB of memory and a few percent of one core), but every room runs the whole game, so --rooms is what sizes the machine. Each room runs on a thread of its own, so the rooms use all the machine's cores, and a room loading a level (when its first player arrives, or when its game loads another) holds up no other room. Players connect and are placed in rooms on the server's main thread meanwhile. With more rooms open than --threads, the rooms share the threads there are: a level loading in one then holds up the others on its thread for that moment.

docs.title: Run it with Docker
docs.text:
Dockerfile.server builds an image holding the server and one game, nothing else:

docker build -f Dockerfile.server --build-arg GAME=games/platformer -t my-game-server .
docker run -d --restart unless-stopped -p 7777:7777 -v my-game-data:/data my-game-server --rooms 4

GAME is the game's folder, relative to the repository. docker compose up server does the same for the platformer (GAME=path/to/game docker compose up server for another). The container runs as an unprivileged user and writes only to /data, where the game's saves are kept (a volume, so that they outlive the container).

docs.title: Put it on the internet
docs.text:
1. Rent any small Linux server with a public address, and install Docker on it (or build RedGem there, see Install).
  2. Copy the repository and your game there, then build and run the image as above.
  3. Open the port: allow TCP 7777 in the server's firewall and in the provider's control panel.
  4. Point the game at it. In the platformer demo, set SERVER in scripts/main_scene.rb; in a game made from the platformer template, set SERVER in scripts/online.rb:
SERVER = "play.example.com".freeze      # or "203.0.113.7", or "play.example.com:9000"

The game's menus then offer Play online. In your own game, it is one line:

Network.join("play.example.com")                  # any room with a free place
Network.join("play.example.com", room: "K7QM3P")  # the room a friend is in

docs.title: Make the game work on a server
docs.text:
The server runs the same scripts as the players, with Network.server? true. It has no player of its own, so whatever a script does for "my player" is skipped there:

Network.on_connect do
  spawn_my_hero unless Network.server?                # the server plays nobody
  Network.players.each { |peer| show_hero_of(peer) }  # the others who play, never the server
end

Network.host? is true on the server: it hosts the game and owns the level's own objects, so what the host decides (scores, a door opening, the end of a match) is decided there. Menus never open on a server. Call Game.quit on the server when a match is over to give its room to the next players.

Save on the server is the server's own: a SQLite database in its data folder (--data), shared by all its rooms and kept across restarts. Each key is a row of its own, written as soon as it changes, in a transaction (a crash keeps every change made before it, never half of one), and only what a script asks for is read into memory. Rooms write one at a time, and change a value that several rooms may change with Save.update, which reads and writes it with no other room's save in between. Arrays and hashes saved there may hold any number of things (only their nesting is limited, to 16 levels). Keep each player's data under their identity, as Online services shows; with many players, a key per player (Save["player:#{identity}"]) reads and writes one player instead of all of them.

A copy of the database for a backup is taken with sqlite3 save.sqlite3 ".backup copy.sqlite3", or by copying the folder while the server is stopped.

The server faces the internet. It keeps every limit a hosted game and the relay have (message sizes, how much each player may send, connections per address, spawned objects), lets go of machines that stay silent and of players who say nothing to the game for five minutes (a game left paused counts), and keeps out addresses that guess at room codes. Messages are not encrypted. Players are let in without asking unless the game decides who plays: see Online services.

docs.title: The editor
docs.text:
./build/src/redgem games/platformer          # opens the editor
./build/src/redgem games/platformer --play   # just plays the game

The editor is built with Dear ImGui (dark theme, Inter and JetBrains Mono fonts, Font Awesome icons):

  • Toolbar: move / rotate / scale gizmos, local or world axes, grid snapping (or hold Ctrl while dragging), Play / Pause / Stop, and Build.
  • Hierarchy: the object tree with search. Click to select, double click to frame, drag onto another object to parent it (or onto empty space to unparent), right click for actions and to create objects. Scripts and models from the Project panel can be dropped on it.
  • Scene: hold the right mouse button and use WASD/QE to fly, wheel to dolly, F to frame the selection, click to pick objects, W / E / R switch the gizmo. Drop a model on the ground to place it there, or a script on an object to attach it.
  • Inspector: name, tag, visible, Template (hidden in the game, copied with Scene.spawn), then one card per component: Transform, Mesh with its materials (color, metallic, roughness, emission), Light (type, color, intensity, range), Camera (field of view, clipping), one card per Ruby script, Physics (body, trigger, collider, mass), vehicle wheels and custom properties. Add Component adds scripts (existing or new), a physics body, a trigger or a property.
  • GameObject menu: terrain you sculpt with a brush (see Levels), empty objects, cube / sphere / plane / cylinder / capsule (with colliders), directional / point / spot lights, cameras, and the game's models.
  • Your own models and sounds: drop .glb files (exported from Blender) and .wav / .ogg / .mp3 / .flac files from your file manager onto the editor window. They are copied into the game's models/ and sounds/ folders and show up in the Project panel.
  • Project: the game's scripts, models, sounds and scenes. Double click a script to edit it, a model to add it to the scene, a sound to hear it. New script creates a Behaviour from a template; Open folder shows the files.
  • Console: engine and Ruby output (filter by level), including script errors with backtraces.
  • Scripts: each open Ruby file gets its own tab next to the Scene. Drag tabs to split the view anywhere (or press Split right), like a code editor's editor groups. Ctrl+S saves and checks the syntax (errors show the line); Open externally uses your default editor. Play saves all open scripts and reloads them.
  • View menu: hide the Hierarchy (Ctrl+B), the Inspector (Ctrl+Alt+B) or the bottom panels (Ctrl+J) to give the scene or the code more room; the toolbar's outer buttons toggle the sides.
  • Play / Pause / Stop (Ctrl+P, Esc): runs the game inside the Scene view with the current edits and fresh scripts; Stop restores the scene exactly as it was.
  • Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y undo and redo, Ctrl+D duplicate, Del delete, Ctrl+S save. Help > Keyboard Shortcuts lists them all. File > New / Open Game goes back to the hub.

Undo goes back up to 200 steps, and keeps at most 256 MB for them (its copies of the objects and terrains, and what deleted objects and undone imports were made of: vertices, pictures and their bytes in the scene's file; an estimate, counted as each step begins): past either, the oldest steps go, and what no step can bring back any more is let go of, so a long session with many imports does not keep growing. The latest step always stays, however big.

Saving rewrites scene.glb in place (only the glTF JSON; meshes and textures are untouched), so the file still opens in Blender. When the file changes on disk (e.g. you re-export from Blender) the editor reloads it automatically, unless you have unsaved edits.

docs.title: Your first game
docs.text: You will create a game from a template, change it, write a behaviour in Ruby and export it.

docs.title: 1. Create the game
docs.text:
Start RedGem with no arguments. In the project hub, pick the Platformer template, type a name and create it. The same from a terminal:

./build/src/redgem new ~/RedGemGames/my_game --template platformer
./build/src/redgem ~/RedGemGames/my_game

With Docker, write tools/docker/editor.sh wherever this manual says ./build/src/redgem.

The editor opens:

  • Scene (center): the level. Hold the right mouse button and use WASD to fly, scroll to move closer, click an object to select it.
  • Hierarchy (left): every object of the level.
  • Inspector (right): what the selected object is made of.
  • Project and Console (bottom): the game's files, and messages from the engine and from your scripts.

docs.title: 2. Play it
docs.text: Press Play in the toolbar (or Ctrl+P). The game runs inside the Scene view: WASD moves, Space jumps. Press Esc or Stop to go back to editing. The level returns exactly to how it was.

docs.title: 3. Change the level
docs.text:
1. Click a coin in the Scene view.
  2. Drag the arrows of the gizmo to move it somewhere harder to reach.
  3. Press Ctrl+D to duplicate it and move the copy too.
  4. Press Ctrl+S to save.

Ctrl+Z undoes any of this.

docs.title: 4. Write a behaviour
docs.text:
Make the hero's coins worth collecting: a platform that moves up and down.

  1. In the menu, GameObject > 3D Object > Cube. Scale and place it as a platform.
  2. In the Inspector, Add Component > Script, type bob and press New.
  3. The script opens in a tab next to the Scene. Replace its contents with:
# Moves the object up and down.
class Bob < Behaviour
  HEIGHT = 2.0   # meters
  SECONDS = 4.0  # per cycle

  def start
    @origin = transform.position
  end

  def update(_dt)
    wave = Math.sin(Time.elapsed / SECONDS * 2 * Math::PI)
    transform.position = @origin + Vector3.up * (wave * HEIGHT)
  end
end
  1. Press Ctrl+S. The tab shows Syntax OK, or the line of the mistake.
  2. With the cube selected, find the Physics card in the Inspector and set Body to kinematic, so the hero can stand on it while it moves.
  3. Press Play.

If a script fails while the game runs, the game keeps going: that behaviour is switched off and the error, with its line, appears in the Console.

docs.title: 5. Share it
docs.text: Build in the toolbar (or redgem build <game> <folder>) makes a folder with your game's executable and its files, for Linux, Windows or (from a Mac) macOS. Zip it and send it. See Building and sharing.

docs.title: Install
docs.text: RedGem is experimental. The editor is developed on Linux; there are Windows and macOS downloads too. Pick one of the ways below.

docs.title: Download (easiest)
docs.text:
System Download Linux (x86_64) redgem-linux-x86_64.tar.gz Windows (x86_64) redgem-windows-x86_64.zip macOS (Apple Silicon) redgem-macos-arm64.zip macOS (Intel) redgem-macos-x86_64.zip

Unpack it anywhere and run bin/redgem (Linux), redgem.exe (Windows) or open RedGem.app (macOS). Nothing is installed: delete the folder to remove it. The demos are in its games/ folder.

  • Linux needs a desktop with OpenGL 3.3, a processor with AVX2 and glibc 2.39 or newer (Ubuntu 24.04 and later). It builds games for Linux, Windows and Android.
  • Windows is compiled from Linux and has only been tried under Wine, not on a real Windows machine yet. It builds games for Windows.
  • macOS needs macOS 11 or newer. It is built and tested on GitHub's Mac machines (macOS 14 on Apple Silicon, macOS 15 on Intel), which are virtual machines with no graphics card OpenGL can use: there the editor opens, edits, plays and saves a game drawn by Apple's software renderer. It has not been tried on a real Mac yet. It builds games for the Mac only. The app is not signed by a registered Apple developer nor notarized, so macOS refuses it the first time: right-click RedGem.app and choose Open (on macOS 15 and later: try once, then System Settings > Privacy & Security > Open Anyway), or run xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine RedGem.app in the unpacked folder.

Wherever this manual says ./build/src/redgem ..., write bin/redgem ... (or redgem.exe ..., or RedGem.app/Contents/MacOS/redgem ... on macOS).

docs.title: With Docker
docs.text:
You need Docker and a desktop session using X11.

git clone https://github.com/carlosdanielpohlod/redgem.git
cd redgem
tools/docker/editor.sh

The first run builds the image, which takes a few minutes. After that the editor opens in seconds.

  • Games you create are saved in ~/RedGemGames on your machine.
  • The demos are in the games/ folder of the checkout: tools/docker/editor.sh games/platformer.
  • The script takes the same arguments as redgem itself, so wherever this manual says ./build/src/redgem ..., write tools/docker/editor.sh .... Paths must be inside ~/RedGemGames or the checkout's games/ folder: the container sees nothing else.
  • The container has no sound.

docs.title: From source
docs.text:
You need a C++17 compiler, CMake 3.24 or newer, Ninja, Ruby with rake, and the X11 and OpenGL development files. On Ubuntu or Debian:

sudo apt install build-essential cmake ninja-build git ca-certificates xz-utils ruby rake bison \
  libgl1-mesa-dev libx11-dev libxrandr-dev libxinerama-dev libxcursor-dev libxi-dev libasound2-dev

On macOS: the Xcode command line tools (xcode-select --install), then brew install cmake ninja and a Ruby with rake (the CI builds with Ruby 3.3).

Then:

cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja
cmake --build build
./build/src/redgem

CMake downloads the libraries RedGem is built on at fixed versions. The first build takes a few minutes.

docs.title: Check that it works
docs.text: ./build/src/redgem (or tools/docker/editor.sh) opens the project hub. Choose Platformer under New game, give it a name, and the editor opens with a level you can play right away: press the Play button, move with WASD, jump with Space.

docs.title: Blender (optional)
docs.text: You can make whole games without it. Install Blender 4.x when you want to model your own objects or build levels there: see Levels, lighting and Blender.

docs.title: How a scene is made
docs.text:
1. Model the level in Blender. Gameplay is configured with custom properties (Object Properties → Custom Properties), e.g. script = "coin.rb", trigger = true.
  2. Export to scene.glb (glTF binary). The exporter writes custom properties to each node's extras.
  3. The runtime loads the .glb with cgltf, reads the extras, builds physics bodies and instantiates the Ruby class named after each script (camera_follow.rb → CameraFollow).

A game is just a folder:

games/platformer/
  scene.glb          # exported from Blender
  platformer.blend   # the editable source
  scripts/*.rb       # behaviours

docs.title: Look of a scene: environment, lights and effects
docs.text:
Scenes are drawn in HDR and finished with bloom (bright things glow), filmic tone mapping, a vignette and anti-aliasing. One object with the property environment = true (GameObject > Environment in the editor, or a Blender empty) sets the mood through its properties:

Property Meaning sky_top, sky_horizon, ground_color colors of the sky gradient, as #rrggbb; they also light the scene fog_color, fog_density distance fog (it follows the horizon color unless given its own) ambient, exposure strength of the sky's light, overall brightness bloom, vignette, sun_glow glow around bright things, dark corners, the sun's disc and halo (0 turns each off) wind how much foliage sways shadows darkness of the sun's shadows (0 = none, 1 = full) ambient_occlusion darkening of creases and contact areas (0 = none, 1 = full) contrast, saturation the finished picture's grade: 1 leaves it as it is grain, aberration film grain, and color fringes toward the corners as through a lens (0 turns each off) sky_image, sky_rotation, sky_intensity a picture of the sky in the game's images/ folder, drawn behind everything and lighting the scene (see "A sky picture"), the degrees it is turned around the vertical, and its brightness (1 = as the picture is) msaa samples per pixel of the scene's picture (2, 4 or 8; 0, the default, is one): smoother edges, and grass and leaves whose cut-out edges are smoothed too antialias "temporal" smooths edges with the frames before (see "Large outdoor scenes"); anything else, the default, smooths them after the picture is drawn shadow_cascades, shadow_distance sun shadows over a large area: 1 to 4 maps, each farther from the camera, reaching shadow_distance meters (150 unless given) shadow_softness how wide the sun is, in degrees: shadows grow softer the farther they fall from what casts them (the real sun is about 0.5; 0, the default, keeps every edge equally soft) glow_limit the brightest glowing particles together make a pixel, in linear light (2 to 4 suits fire): many flames or sparks over each other come near it and keep their color instead of washing out to white (0, the default, sets no limit)

Without one, scenes get a clear day. Other things worth knowing: the 16 point lights nearest to the camera are used each frame (so a street can have dozens of lamps); the sun casts soft shadows around the camera; and materials use their glTF normal, roughness/metallic, occlusion and emission textures. A light's intensity and color can change while the game runs (see Gameplay recipes).

docs.title: See-through materials and wind
docs.text:
Blender's material settings decide how a material shows what is behind it (the glTF exporter writes them as the material's alpha mode):

Alpha mode Drawn as For Opaque whole: its alpha is not looked at almost everything Mask (alpha clip) cut out where its alpha is below the material's cutoff leaves, grass, fences Blend see-through: mixed with what is behind it by its alpha glass, hair cards, fur, smoke on a card

A blended material is drawn in two steps. What of it is nearly opaque (alpha 0.9 and above) is drawn with the opaque surfaces, so that a dozen hair cards over each other still sort themselves out; the rest is drawn after every opaque surface, mixed with what is behind it, one object at a time from the farthest to the nearest. Two see-through parts of the same object are not sorted between themselves, nor are copies scattered with Scatter.place. For many layers of fine cards (fur, a mane), give the material the custom property transparency = "dithered" (Material Properties → Custom Properties, exported when the exporter's Custom Properties is on): its texels are then left out in a fine pattern that thins with their alpha, which needs no sorting at all, at the price of a slight grain.

Wind. Textured cut-out and blended materials are foliage: drawn on both sides, and swaying with the environment's wind. An object whose foliage must stay still gives itself sway = false; objects moved by a skeleton (characters, and so their hair) do not sway unless they say sway = true. Copies scattered from an object sway as it does.

Glossy surfaces reflect their surroundings: the engine keeps capturing the scene around the camera (one cube face per frame) and uses it for reflections and ambient light.

A sky picture. sky_image = "meadow_sky" puts a picture of the whole sky around the scene (images/meadow_sky.hdr, .png or .jpg): an equirectangular picture, twice as wide as it is high, the kind sites of free skies offer and Blender takes as a world texture. It is laid as Blender lays it (the middle of the picture toward +X; sky_rotation turns it), and it lights the scene in place of the gradient: matte surfaces take the light of the sky around them, and glossy ones reflect it, sharper the smoother they are. Give the picture's sun a sun light of its own pointing the same way (the picture's own sun is held down in the light it gives, so that it does not light the scene twice) and set ambient to 1 for the sky's light as the picture has it. A Radiance picture (.hdr) holds light brighter than white, as a real sky has; a PNG or JPEG stops at white, and sky_intensity makes up for it. Pictures are read up to 8192 pixels a side; the sky drawn behind everything is kept at 4096 pixels across, its light is worked out from a smaller copy when the scene is loaded (a fraction of a second).

Large outdoor scenes. With shadow_cascades = 4 the sun's shadows reach shadow_distance meters, sharp up close and coarser far away; shadow_softness = 1.5 widens their edges with the distance to what casts them (a tree's shadow is sharp at its trunk and soft at its crown). Each cascade draws the scene's casters once more: a forest of tens of thousands of copies costs more with four than with one. msaa = 4 smooths edges with four samples a pixel; cut-out materials (grass, leaves) then let those samples smooth their edges too, which keeps a meadow from shimmering as the camera moves. Without it, cut-out edges are smoothed afterwards with the rest of the picture.

antialias = "temporal" goes further: each frame the view moves by less than a pixel, a different amount every frame, and the frames before, followed to where each pixel was then, are mixed into this one. Thin grass, leaves and the glints of shiny surfaces stop shimmering, and copies fading out by distance turn from a fine pattern into an even shade. What moves is followed, characters' bones and swaying foliage included; what is no longer there (a lightning flash, a character running past, the camera cutting to another place) is not smeared over the picture; particles take less of the frames before. A new scene, a new window size and a camera that jumps start over. It works with msaa on or off and costs one more pass over the scene's opaque surfaces.

Animated characters. glTF skeletons and animations are supported: skinned meshes are deformed on the GPU (up to 1024 bones per skeleton, 4 per vertex: a character with fingers has about 65) and every animation in the scene plays in a loop until a script says otherwise (see Control animations). The editor keeps skeletons and animations when saving, reordering or importing models. tools/blender/walk_rig.py gives a scanned standing person leg bones and a walk cycle.

Per-object color. The property tint = "#rrggbb" multiplies the colors of an object's mesh, so copies sharing one mesh (cars, crates) can each have their own color.

No shadow. cast_shadow = false keeps an object out of the sun's shadows (a sky dome, a glow, a light's shade): it is still drawn and still receives shadows.

Graphics card. On laptops with two cards the engine asks for the dedicated one and logs which card it got. To choose: Edit > Graphics Card in the editor (saved in ~/.config/redgem/settings.json, used from the next start), the REDGEM_GPU environment variable (read by redgem and redgem-test), or --gpu auto|dedicated|integrated for one run. The command line wins over the environment, which wins over the saved setting.

Performance. Objects outside the view, and parts too small to see from where the camera is, are not drawn. Objects that share a mesh (linked duplicates in Blender, Alt+D, or copies of one model) and come one after the other in the level are drawn together, every copy of a part in one call, however many there are: a street of the same building costs little more than one. Blender keeps duplicates together by their names (Tree, Tree.001, Tree.002...); copies whose turn comes between other objects are drawn in that order, so that surfaces lying on each other look as they did. What still costs is the number of different meshes on screen, and of separate parts in each: join the parts of a model that share a material, and give heavy models lighter versions for far away with visible_from and visible_to.

docs.title: Grass, forests and cities
docs.text:
Tens of thousands of copies (a meadow's grass, a forest) are too many to be objects: a script scatters them instead (Scatter.place, see the API reference). Model one tuft or one tree, give it prefab = true so the template itself is hidden in the game, and scatter it over the ground from a scene script's setup:

Scatter.place("GrassTuft", count: 50_000, area: [Vector3[-80, 0, -80], Vector3[80, 0, 80]],
              ground: find("Ground"), seed: 7, scale: 0.7..1.4, align: true)
Scatter.place("Tree", count: 2_000, area: [Vector3[-140, 0, -140], Vector3[140, 0, -90]],
              ground: find("Ground"), seed: 8, scale: 0.8..1.5)

The copies take the template's own mesh (a model whose parts are children: join them), its scale, tint, visible_from / visible_to and cast_shadow. They are only drawn: nothing collides with them (give the trees a collider of their own, or invisible objects, where players must not walk through) and no script runs on them. The same seed places them the same on every machine of a game.

They are drawn by patches of ground 16 m across: a patch out of view, or too far for its biggest copy to show, is skipped whole. Like any object, they cast shadows, and small things (grass) only near the camera: a tuft half a meter high stops casting one about 50 m away, a tree hundreds of meters away. Their foliage sways in the wind (wind on the environment), each copy with its own phase, so a field does not move in step.

How the copies look can vary too, the same for the same seed on every machine:

Scatter.place("GrassTuft", count: 50_000, area: field, ground: find("Ground"), seed: 7, align: true,
              tints: [[0.85, 1.0, 0.7], [1.05, 1.0, 0.8]],  # each a color between these
              tint_variation: 0.12,                         # and a little brighter or darker
              fade: 10.0,                                   # fading out over the last 10 m
              normals_up: 0.7)                              # lit as the meadow, not as flat cards

fade makes copies near the template's visible_to thin out pixel by pixel over that many meters instead of popping away (and fade in after its visible_from, when it has one: two levels of detail whose distances overlap by the fade cross over without a gap). normals_up bends the copies' normals toward their own up: grass cards are then lit as the ground they stand on, so a field does not show the cards' faces turning light and dark with the sun.

docs.title: Terrain
docs.text:
GameObject > Terrain adds a square of ground, 100 m across, that you shape with a brush. It comes selected with the brush on: mountains, holes and plateaus are a drag of the mouse away.

  1. Drag the left mouse button over the ground in the Scene view. A ring shows the brush.
  2. In the Inspector's Terrain card, pick what the brush does (Sculpt turns the brush off and on again, to move the terrain itself with the gizmo):
Brush Effect Raise Piles ground up under the brush (hold Shift to dig instead) Lower Digs (hold Shift to pile up) Smooth Softens bumps and edges Flatten Levels the ground to the height at the brush's center: plateaus, roads

Radius is the size of the brush in meters, Strength how fast it works. Each stroke is one undo step. Untick Sculpt to select and move objects again.

The terrain's collider follows its shape, so characters walk and things roll on the hills you make. Its color and roughness are in the Mesh card, like any object's. A terrain is made and shaped in the editor; one re-exported from Blender is an ordinary mesh.

docs.title: Editing the level in Blender
docs.text:
blender games/platformer/platformer.blend           # edit, save
blender -b games/platformer/platformer.blend \
  --python tools/blender/export_scene.py -- games/platformer/scene.glb

tools/blender/run.sh build_platformer.py games/platformer (or build_driving.py games/driving) regenerates a whole level from code; tools/blender/scene_kit.py has helpers to build levels with bpy.

docs.title: Custom properties
docs.text:
Property Values Meaning script "player.rb" or "a.rb, b.rb" Behaviours to attach, loaded from scripts/ body static, dynamic, kinematic, character, vehicle Physics body (characters use Jolt's CharacterVirtual, vehicles its VehicleConstraint) wheel true On a child of a vehicle: it becomes a wheel (model it with its axle along X) collider box, sphere, capsule, mesh Shape, sized from the mesh bounds × object scale. collider alone = static body trigger true Trigger volume: fires on_trigger_enter/exit, does not collide mass number Mass of dynamic bodies tag string Used by Scene.find_all(tag) and game_object.tag? visible false Hide the mesh (the object still exists) prefab true A template: hidden and inert in the game, copied by Scene.spawn visible_from, visible_to meters The object is drawn only while that far from the camera: give a model a detailed version up close and a light one far away tint "#rrggbb" Multiplies the colors of this object's mesh (copies sharing a mesh can differ) cast_shadow false Keeps the object out of the sun's shadows (a sky dome) sway true / false Whether the wind sways its foliage: unless said, yes, except on objects a skeleton moves (see "See-through materials and wind") environment true This object's properties set the sky, fog and effects (see "Look of a scene") anything number / string / bool Available in Ruby as props[:name] / prop(:name, default)

Cameras and lights (sun, point) are taken from the Blender scene. Spot lights are loaded but lit like point lights (in every direction). Parenting is preserved.

Vehicles. Give the chassis body = "vehicle" and parent the wheel meshes to it with wheel = true. Wheels in front of the center (Blender +Y) steer, the rear ones get the hand brake, and every axle is driven. Wheel radius and width come from the wheel mesh. See tools/blender/build_driving.py. Blender is Z-up; the engine is Y-up like glTF: Blender (x, y, z) is engine (x, z, -y) (Vector3.blender(x, y, z) does the conversion). Forward is -Z (Blender +Y).

docs.title: Building and sharing
docs.text:
Build in the editor's toolbar, or from a terminal:

./build/src/redgem build my_game dist/my_game

This makes a folder with an executable named after your game (dist/my_game/my_game) and a game/ folder with its files. Whoever receives the folder runs the executable: they do not need RedGem, Ruby or Blender installed.

That executable is the player: a copy of redgem-player, a small program that plays the game in the game/ folder beside it and does nothing else. The editor, the project hub and the other tools you make the game with are not in it. A build looks for the player beside the redgem program that builds: redgem-player in the same folder for the system you are on, and runtimes/<system>/ in that folder for the others (runtimes/windows/redgem-player.exe, runtimes/android/<abi>/libredgem.so). When one is missing the build says which file it looked for.

docs.title: For Windows
docs.text:
On Linux, RedGem builds games for Linux, Windows and Android (the experimental Windows download builds Windows games, the macOS one Mac games: --target macos). In the editor, Build asks which one; from a terminal:

tools/windows/build_runtime.sh                                   # once: builds the player for Windows
./build/src/redgem build my_game dist/my_game_win --target windows

The first command downloads a Windows compiler into the project (no administrator rights needed) and builds redgem-player.exe into build/src/runtimes/windows/; it takes a few minutes and is only needed once, or again after updating RedGem. The build then makes dist/my_game_win/my_game.exe next to its game/ folder. It needs 64-bit Windows 10 or later and a graphics card with OpenGL 3.3; nothing has to be installed with it.

docs.title: For Android
docs.text:
tools/android/build_runtime.sh                                   # once: builds the player for Android
./build/src/redgem build my_game dist/my_game_android --target android

The result is dist/my_game_android/my_game.apk, with the game's files inside it. Install it on a phone with adb install, or copy the file to the phone and open it. tools/android/run_on_device.sh my_game builds, installs, starts the game on the phone or emulator that adb sees, and shows its log.

What it needs on your machine:

  • The Android SDK with its build-tools and one platform (sdkmanager "build-tools;35.0.0" "platforms;android-35"), and ANDROID_HOME pointing at it.
  • Java (the SDK's signing tool runs on it).
  • The first command downloads the Android compiler (NDK) into the project and builds the engine for phones (arm64) and for emulators (x86_64); it takes several minutes, once.

What changes on a phone:

  • The game fills the screen: it keeps the height from game.json and gets the width that fits.
  • Touch controls appear by themselves and act as a gamepad: a stick under the left thumb, A and B under the right, Start in the corner. A game that plays with a gamepad plays on a phone as it is; taps also work as mouse clicks, so UI.button menus work. A game with a touch interface of its own hides them with Input.touch_controls = false.
  • Characters may have as many bones on a phone as on a computer (up to 1024 per skeleton).
  • There is no on-screen keyboard yet, so text fields cannot be typed in.
  • Phones are slower than computers: keep levels light (few lights, modest textures) and test on a real device. It needs Android 8 or later with OpenGL ES 3.
  • The APK is signed with a key the engine makes on your machine the first time (~/.config/redgem/android-debug.keystore). It never leaves your machine and is different on everyone's; it is good for your own devices and for sharing the file.

docs.title: Your own app id, version and key
docs.text:
A game says these in the android section of its game.json; all are optional:

{
  "title": "My Game",
  "android": {
    "package": "com.mystudio.mygame",
    "version_code": 3,
    "version_name": "1.2",
    "keystore": "../keys/release.keystore",
    "key_alias": "mygame"
  }
}
  • package is the app's id on the phone. Without it the app goes by the game's id (see below), and a game with no id by its folder name.
  • version_code goes up with every release: a phone only updates to a higher one.
  • keystore and key_alias sign the app with a key of your own, which is what a release needs: players can only update a game signed with the same key as the one they have. Make it once with Java's keytool and keep it safe (and backed up): there is no getting it back.
  • The key's password is never written in a file. Give it when building:
REDGEM_KEYSTORE_PASSWORD='...' ./build/src/redgem build my_game dist/android --target android

(REDGEM_KEY_PASSWORD too, when the key has a password of its own.) - Keep the keystore outside the game's folder. If one is left there anyway, builds leave it out: a signing key never travels with a game.

docs.title: Recording a video
docs.text:
redgem <game_dir> --record out.mp4 plays the game into a video. You need ffmpeg on the PATH; without it RedGem says so and does not start.

redgem games/arena --record trailer.mp4 --record-fps 30 --record-size 3840x2160 --record-scale 1920x1080 --record-seconds 20
  • Each frame moves the game on by exactly 1/--record-fps seconds (30 unless given), however long it takes to draw. A scene too heavy to play smoothly still comes out smooth in the video, and so do the wind, film grain and everything else that moves with time.
  • --record-size is the size the game is drawn at, off screen (the window's own size unless given). It is not limited by the window or the desktop, and the window shows a fitted copy. --record-scale sets the video's size; frames are scaled down to it with lanczos, so drawing at 4K and scaling to 1080p gives very clean edges.
  • Recording ends after --record-seconds, when a script calls Game.stop_recording (the game keeps running in the window), or when the game quits.
  • Frames are read back from the graphics card a few frames late, so drawing never waits for it. They are encoded as H.264 (-crf 16, preset medium, yuv420p), which plays everywhere.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The executable needs the game/ folder next to it.
  • game.json says what the game is and how its window opens:
{ "id": "com.mystudio.mygame", "title": "My Game", "window_width": 1280, "window_height": 720 }

  • id is what the game is known by: its save follows it when the folder is moved or renamed, and its Android app is named after it. redgem new writes one (my-game-3fa2c1b0); change it to your own before the first release and leave it alone after. It is small letters, digits, ., - and _, starting and ending with a letter or a digit. Two games with the same id share a save: a game started as a copy of another needs a new one. A game with no id keeps its save by where its folder is, and starts a new save when it is given one.

  • Everything in the game folder is copied, including the scripts as plain .rb files.

  • Check the licenses of the models and sounds you include. A license that allows using an asset in a game does not always allow shipping its original file.

docs.title: Installing RedGem somewhere else
docs.text:
cmake --install build --component redgem --prefix <folder> copies the programs out of the build folder, laid out the way builds expect:

<folder>/bin/redgem            the editor, the project hub and the command line
<folder>/bin/redgem-player     what a game built for this system is a copy of
<folder>/bin/redgem-relay      the meeting point for games over the internet
<folder>/bin/redgem-server     runs a game on a server, for players to join (see Dedicated server)
<folder>/bin/redgem-test       the tool that runs a game's tests
<folder>/bin/runtimes/         the players for other systems that were built before installing

docs.title: Testing your game
docs.text:
The example below tests the game made in Your first game.

A system test is a Ruby script that plays your game: it holds keys, waits, checks what happened and can take screenshots. It runs the real game, frame by frame, at the same pace on any machine.

# tests/collect_coin_test.rb
SystemTest.define do |t|
  t.wait(30)                                   # frames
  t.hold(:w, frames: 60)                       # walk forward for a second
  t.wait_until(frames: 30) { Scene.find("Coin1").nil? }
  t.assert("the score counts the coin") { Scene.find("Player").get_component(Player).coins == 1 }
  t.screenshot("coin_collected")
end

Run it with redgem-test, the program that runs tests (it is built next to redgem):

./build/src/redgem-test my_game tests/collect_coin_test.rb --screenshots shots

The command exits with an error when an assertion fails or a script raises, so it fits in any automated check. Add --headless to run without opening a window (no screenshots then); redgem-test --help lists every option.

redgem-test is a development tool. It is not part of a built game: the program your players receive (what redgem build and the editor's Build make) contains no test code at all, and SystemTest and the rest of what tests are written with do not exist in the Ruby your game runs in. They are only there while redgem-test plays it.

docs.title: What a test can do
docs.text:
Call Effect t.wait(frames) Lets the game run t.hold(:w, :a, frames: 60) Holds keys for that long t.press(:space) Taps a key t.move_mouse(x, y), t.click(x, y) Moves the mouse; clicks there with the left button t.type("Ana") Types a text (what Input.text and UI.text_field read) t.tilt(:left_y, -1.0, frames: 60) Pushes a gamepad stick (or pulls a trigger) for that long t.press_button(:a), t.hold_button(:a, frames: 30) Taps or holds gamepad buttons t.hold_until(:w, frames: 300) { ... } Holds keys until the block is true t.wait_until(frames: 120) { ... } Waits until the block is true, or fails t.assert("message") { ... } Fails the test when the block is false t.screenshot("name") Saves a picture of the next frame as name.png in the screenshots folder (--screenshots <dir>, screenshots unless said)

Inside the blocks you have the whole scripting API, so a test can also move objects or read any behaviour's state. Taking pictures is something only tests do: a game's own scripts have no call for it. What the game saves with Save goes to a file of the test's own, which starts empty: a test never sees or changes your real progress.

docs.title: Testing Ruby code by itself
docs.text:
Code that needs no running game (a formula, a helper class) can be tested without one. A file of unit tests defines classes that inherit from RedGemTest::Case; every method whose name starts with test_ is a test:

# tests/score_test.rb
class ScoreTest < RedGemTest::Case
  def test_a_coin_is_worth_ten_points
    assert_equal 10, 1 * 10
    assert_in_delta 0.5, Vector3.new(0.5, 0, 0).length
  end
end

./build/src/redgem-test --ruby tests/score_test.rb

It runs in the same Ruby a game runs in, with the scripting API and an empty scene. The assertions are assert, refute, assert_equal, assert_nil, assert_in_delta, assert_vector and assert_raises; a system test has them too.

To test the game's own classes, say which game they are from: they then load by name from its scripts folder, as they do when the game runs (without --game, from the test file's folder).

./build/src/redgem-test --ruby tests/score_test.rb --game .

A test may reopen one of the game's classes to add to it, a trace or a stand-in for a method:

# tests/fighter_trace_test.rb
class Fighter
  alias untraced_strike strike
  def strike(*args) = (Debug.log("strike #{args.inspect}"); untraced_strike(*args))
end

A class or module line at the top of the file (not indented) loads that class from the game's scripts first, so the line reopens the game's Fighter instead of making a new, empty one.

docs.title: What RedGem does not do yet
docs.text:
Knowing this up front saves time:

  • Input is keyboard, mouse and one gamepad. Keys and buttons cannot be rebound by the player.
  • In-game interface is texts, rectangles, images, buttons and text fields you draw each frame. There are no sliders or layout containers.
  • Particles are let out in bursts, as dots or pictures. They do not collide and are not lit.
  • Animation: a character plays one clip with a second mixed over it. There are no blend trees, no animation events and no inverse kinematics.
  • Multiplayer has no matchmaking and no lag compensation; playing over the internet needs a relay you run, or a forwarded port (see Multiplayer).
  • Platforms: the editor is developed on Linux; the Windows and macOS downloads are experimental (macOS has only run on GitHub's virtual Macs, drawn by Apple's software renderer). Games are built for Linux, Windows and Android, and for the Mac from the Mac's editor (no iOS, no web).
  • macOS says the app cannot be opened ("unidentified developer", or "damaged"): the app is not signed by a registered Apple developer. Right-click RedGem.app and choose Open (on macOS 15 and later: System Settings > Privacy & Security > Open Anyway), or run xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine RedGem.app in the unpacked folder.
  • Scripts are loaded when you press Play; they are not reloaded while the game runs.
  • Scene size: a scene (or a model) that would need more than 4 GB of memory, counting its file, its vertices as the engine keeps them and its pictures as they are once decoded, is refused with a message saying how much it needs. The biggest demo scene comes to about 1.8 GB. This is an estimate of the memory the game holds, not a limit on the graphics card's memory.

docs.title: Common problems
docs.text:
The editor does not open from Docker. Your session must use X11 (echo $XDG_SESSION_TYPE prints x11). The launcher tools/docker/editor.sh allows the container on your display and removes that permission when the editor closes.

The build fails looking for X11 headers. Install the development packages listed in Install. If you cannot install packages, tools/setup/fetch_x11_headers.sh extracts the headers into the project.

My script does nothing. Look at the Console: a script with an error is switched off and reported there. Check that the class name matches the file name (moving_door.rb defines MovingDoor) and that it inherits from Behaviour.

on_trigger_enter never fires. The object needs Trigger on, and the thing entering must be a character, a dynamic body or a kinematic body. Static scenery does not set triggers off.

The hero falls through a platform I move from a script. Give the platform a kinematic body. A static body is not meant to move.

The game is slow on a laptop with two graphics cards. RedGem asks for the dedicated card and logs which one it got when it starts. To choose: Edit > Graphics Card in the editor, or start with --gpu dedicated.

Joining fails with "this game runs protocol 1, the other side 2". The two machines (or the game and the relay or server it meets on) run versions of RedGem whose network messages differ. Build every copy of the game, the relay and the server from the same version.

I want to see what the machines of a game say to each other. Start the game, the relay or the server with REDGEM_LOG_MESSAGES=1 in its environment: every message it sends and receives is written to its log, as JSON text.

I changed the level in Blender and the editor did not update. It reloads scene.glb by itself when you have no unsaved edits. With unsaved edits it asks.

Script errors are logged with a backtrace and only disable the failing behaviour; the game keeps running. Every native takes finite numbers a float can hold: infinity, NaN (0.0 / 0.0) or a number too large (1e300) raises an ArgumentError instead of reaching the scene.
